name: Nora Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a free-range egg farm, 16,000 hens in two sheds, owned by the Whitlock family. I start at half six, walk the sheds, pick up the floor eggs, the ones the hens lay in the litter instead of the nest boxes, and check for any dead or poorly birds. Then it's the packing room, feeding trays into the grader, which sorts the eggs by size, and stacking boxes for the lorry. Afternoons I open the pop holes so the hens can get out on the range, and close them at dusk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same every day. Hens don't care if it's Christmas, and I find that oddly restful. What wears me out is the dust in the sheds and the worry about bird flu, because two winters ago we had to keep them all shut in for months and Mr Whitlock was talking about cutting hours. My partner Luc drives a parcel van, and between us we get by, with a bit put away, about two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine with me. I've never used any of those AI things and I don't feel I've missed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss. People get worked up over every new thing and most of it comes to nothing. I'm not one for posting online, so I'd just say it in the packing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a weight off. I'm not quick with new stuff and I know it. Bird flu's my monster. I don't need a second one in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Try to get the savings up from two months to four, because the bird flu scare showed me how quickly hours can go. Maybe ask Mr Whitlock if I can learn the grader's settings, since only Denise knows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if hours did get cut for other reasons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's a business, eggs are cheap, the supermarkets set the price. You can moan about it but it doesn't change anything, so I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said only Denise knows the grader. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Denise is 60 and she'll retire. If I knew the grader, I'd be harder to let go. That's about as far as my planning goes, to be honest.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, all that fuss for nothing, since most new things come to nothing. I'd say it in the packing room rather than online.
S0.think: It'd be a weight off, because I'm not quick with new things. Bird flu is already my big worry and I don't need a second one.
S0.do: Carries on at the egg farm and tries to raise savings from two months to four. Asks the owner to let her learn the egg grader's settings before the older colleague who runs it retires.
S0.quote: Bird flu's my monster. I don't need a second one in the shed.
S0.fieldNote: Nora's real fear is bird flu, which once threatened her hours, and AI barely registers next to it. She blames no one for low pay, seeing it as just how business works. Her one plan is to learn the grader so she's harder to let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. They do have those robots now that drive round the shed floor picking up eggs. A rep came round last spring with a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if it saves my back, fine, as long as there's still a job at the end of it. I'd keep it short. I don't like getting into arguments about it at work, there's always someone who gets heated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the floor eggs are about a third of my morning. If a robot does that, Mr Whitlock either finds me something else or cuts my hours. I'd guess cut hours, because that's what he does when things are tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back where we can, takeaways, the gym I never go to, and put more aside. I wouldn't go looking for a course or anything, I'd keep my head down and do my job well so he's got no reason to pick me. If the hours did go, I'd look at the other egg farm out on the main road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. That low, background kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is that a plan, or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I'm not going to beat a robot at picking up eggs. I'm just hoping to be cheaper than it for a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Luc say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he's more worried about his van, because they keep talking about self-driving ones. We'd have a quiet night in and work out the numbers on the back of an envelope. We always do that when something's bothering us.

S1.say: I'd say if it saves my back, fine, as long as there's still a job at the end. I'd keep it short to avoid arguments at work.
S1.think: Floor eggs are a third of my morning, so a robot means my boss either finds me other work or cuts my hours, and I'd guess cuts. I can't beat a robot, I can only hope to be cheaper for a while.
S1.do: Cuts small costs like takeaways and an unused gym membership and puts more aside. Avoids courses and keeps her head down, and would look at another egg farm nearby if her hours went.
S1.quote: I'm not going to beat a robot at picking up eggs. I'm just hoping to be cheaper than it for a while longer.
S1.fieldNote: Nora's strategy is to be cheaper than the robot and avoid being noticed, which she admits is part hope. She avoids conflict and doesn't want to argue about AI at work. Her partner's van job is just as exposed, so the couple's risk is doubled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's both of us, me and Luc. The robot for the eggs and the robot for the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope somebody up there's got a plan, because I haven't. That'd be about it, I'm not one for marches. Maybe I'd sign a petition if someone sent me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. We've got two months saved and two jobs that a machine can do, and no idea what else we'd be good for. I'd keep thinking about my nan, who lost her job at the textile mill and never really worked again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything we didn't need straight away. Ask my mum and dad if we could move into their spare room to save the rent, they're only twenty minutes away. And sign up for whatever the government offered, I wouldn't be proud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in the stomach, like when the vet came about bird flu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your nan.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She was 50 when the mill shut. She did some cleaning, then some childminding, but she always said she'd lost her place. I don't want to be my nan at 29, sitting in my mum's spare room waiting for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for marches. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd sign things and I'd vote for whoever promised to pay people. But standing in the street isn't me, I'd feel daft.

S2.say: I'd say I hope somebody up there has a plan, because I haven't. I might sign a petition if someone sent me one, but that's about it.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, with two months saved and two jobs a machine can do. I keep thinking of my nan, who lost her mill job and never really worked again.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending at once and asks her parents about moving into their spare room to save rent. Signs up for any government support on offer.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick in the stomach, like the day the vet came about bird flu.
S2.quote: I don't want to be my nan at 29, sitting in my mum's spare room waiting for a letter.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario hits Nora's household twice, since both she and her partner do work machines could take. Her grandmother's job loss at a mill is the story she reaches for. She'd accept help and vote for it but wouldn't protest, which fits her centre, conflict-avoiding style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Though I'd probably spend the first two pretending it wasn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better start getting ready, all of us, not just leave it to the government. I'd say it in a calm way. People round here don't like being told the sky's falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know I should do something and I'd find reasons not to. It's always next month with me. But I'd at least save, because saving's the one thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save hard, aim for six months by the time it lands. Luc and I were going to get married next summer, and I think I'd want to make it small, register office and a meal, and put the rest in the bank. I'd probably stay at the egg farm until they told me to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the night before a test you haven't revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Luc feel about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be relieved, honestly. It was my mum who wanted the big do. We'd still be married, that's the main thing, and money in the bank is worth more than a disco.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay until they told you to go. Why not leave earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where would I go? Every job I could do is on the list. There's no point jumping off one boat if all the other boats are sinking at the same time. At least at Whitlock's I know the work.

S3.say: I'd say we'd better start getting ready ourselves instead of leaving it all to the government. I'd say it calmly, because people here don't like being told the sky's falling.
S3.think: I'd know I should act and find reasons not to, because it's always next month with me. Saving is the one thing I'd definitely do.
S3.do: Saves toward six months of expenses and scales the planned wedding down to a register office and a meal. Stays at the egg farm until told to go.
S3.feel: Anxious, like the night before a test she hasn't studied for.
S3.quote: There's no point jumping off one boat if all the other boats are sinking at the same time.
S3.fieldNote: Nora is candid that she'd waste the early years of warning, putting things off until next month. Shrinking the wedding is her clearest concrete change. She sees no point moving jobs if every job she could do is exposed, which is a logical reason for her staying put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? That's a long way off. I'd be 37. I can't really picture 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and people should stop worrying. Somebody would sort it out by then. That's what most people round here would say, and I'd go along with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the same, mostly, and that's the trouble. Ten years out it's the government's problem. Five years out it's mine and Luc's. Two years out it's already happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, carry on. Keep saving a bit, learn the grader, maybe think about kids in a few years like we planned. I'd start worrying properly around year six or seven, I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just faintly. It'd sit in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could make yourself act earlier, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe learn something with people instead of hens, like working in a school kitchen or a care home. But you said robots would do hands-on things too, so I don't know. That's partly why I wouldn't bother early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So does more warning help you or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps the people who plan. I'm not one of them. For me, the ten-year one is the comfiest to hear about and probably the worst to live through, because I'd do nothing until it was close.

S4.say: I'd say there's plenty of time and someone would sort it out by then. Most people round here would say that and I'd go along with it.
S4.think: Privately I'd think much the same, which is the trouble. Ten years out it's the government's problem, five years out it's ours, and two years out it's already happened.
S4.do: Carries on at the egg farm, saves a little, learns the grader and keeps a loose plan for children in a few years. Expects to start worrying properly only around year six or seven.
S4.feel: Faintly uneasy, a worry sitting at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: Ten years out it's the government's problem. Five years out it's mine and Luc's. Two years out it's already happened.
S4.fieldNote: Nora explained clearly how distance in time removes urgency for her, passing the problem from government to household to something already done. She thinks the ten-year version is the most comfortable to hear and the worst to live through. Without a nearby, visible threat she'd make no changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes Luc's job and mine at the same time and we've got two months saved. What would help is the government just paying people a wage for a while, no forms that take six weeks, and a person at the job centre who actually knows what jobs are left.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens. Nobody ever does. I don't know what a robot would do on a bird flu morning, when you're the one who has to walk in and see them, but I'd like to know someone's thought about it.

headlineQuote: Ten years out it's the government's problem. Five years out it's mine and Luc's. Two years out it's already happened.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old junior worker on a 16,000-hen free-range egg farm, living with a partner who drives a parcel van, with about two months of savings. She's a practical centrist who never uses AI, dislikes conflict, and blames no one for how business works. Her biggest everyday fear is bird flu, not technology. Across the scenarios she cuts back, saves and keeps her head down, hoping to stay cheaper than a robot, and she'd lean on her parents if both jobs went. She is unusually honest that more warning time wouldn't help her much, because she wouldn't act until the threat was close.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because it would take both her job and her partner's at once with only two months saved.
whatWouldHelp: The government paying people a wage for a while without slow forms, and a real person at the job centre who knows which jobs are left.
